subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Three boxes B₁, B₂ and B₃ contain balls with different colours as shown: B₁ has 2 white, 1 black, 2 red; B₂ has 3 white, 2 black, 4 red; B₃ has 4 white, 3 black, 2 red. A die is thrown and B₁ is chosen if either 1 or 2 turns up; B₂ is chosen if 3 or 4 turns up and B₃ is chosen if 5 or 6 turns up. Having chosen a box in this way, a ball is chosen at random from this box. If the ball drawn is of red colour, what is the probability that it comes from box B₂?

mark_split.label: Prior probabilities of choosing each container
Probability of the colour from each container

Answer checked: P(R|B₁) = 2/5, P(R|B₂) = 4/9, P(R|B₃) = 2/9; P(R) = (1/3)(2/5 + 4/9 + 2/9) = (1/3)(16/15) = 16/45; P(B₂|R) = (4/27)/(16/45) = 5/12 — agrees with the book, which reaches 5/12 through 48/45 and 20/48. The book's "(18 + 20 + 10)/(5 × 9)" is the same bracket 2/5 + 4/9 + 2/9 = 48/45 = 16/15 written over 45.

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the probability that the red ball came from B₂ — the events, why each box has prior 1/3, the three red-ball probabilities, the total, and Bayes.
insider_note: The die changes nothing: two faces out of six for each box is 1/3, the same as choosing a box at random. The fractions 2/5, 4/9, 2/9 have two different denominators, so the total needs the common denominator 45.

steps.label: Define the events
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three box events and one colour event, as in every question of this family.

lines.text: Let B₁, B₂, B₃ be the events of choosing the
boxes B₁, B₂, B₃ respectively, and let R be the
event that the ball drawn is red.

recall.must_convey: That B₁, B₂, B₃ are the events of choosing each box and R is the event that the drawn ball is red.
accept: let B one B two B three be choosing each box and R be drawing a red ball
define an event for each box and one event for red
B one B two B three are the box events and R is red
moodu boxes ki B one B two B three events, red ball ki R
name the three box events and the red ball event
heard_as: B one B two B three

steps.why: Exactly one box is chosen by the die, so the three box events are mutually exclusive and exhaustive — the Eᵢ of Bayes' theorem.
common_mistakes: Defining events for the die faces instead of for the boxes.

steps.label: Priors
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Each box is chosen on 2 of the 6 faces: 2/6 = 1/3. Write the reason — the die is what the question changed.

lines.text: Each box is chosen when 2 of the 6 faces

recall.must_convey: That each box is chosen on 2 of the 6 die faces, so P(B₁) = P(B₂) = P(B₃) = 1/3.
accept: each box is chosen on two faces out of six so the prior is one third each
P of B one equals P B two equals P B three equals two by six which is one by three
the die gives each box a third
prathi box ki die lo two faces, so probability 2 by 6 ante one by three
two of six faces for each box so a third

steps.why: The die fixes the box before any ball is seen; the prior is the die's share of faces for that box, and here the shares are equal.
common_mistakes: Taking P(Bᵢ) = 1/6 because a die has six faces.
Weighting the boxes by their ball counts (5, 9, 9).

steps.label: P(red | each box)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. B₁: 2 red of 5. B₂: 4 red of 9. B₃: 2 red of 9.

accept: red given B one is two by five, given B two four by nine, given B three two by nine
the red probabilities are two fifths four ninths and two ninths
P of R given each box is 2 by 5, 4 by 9 and 2 by 9
B one lo red 2 by 5, B two lo 4 by 9, B three lo 2 by 9
two of five, four of nine, two of nine

steps.why: The box totals are 5, 9 and 9, so the denominators differ. Each conditional probability is read inside its own box.
common_mistakes: Using the grand total 23 as every denominator.
Writing the red count of B₃ as 4 (its white count).

steps.label: Total probability of red
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Factor out 1/3, then add 2/5 + 4/9 + 2/9 over 45: 18 + 20 + 10 = 48, so the bracket is 48/45 = 16/15 and P(R) = 16/45.

accept: P of R is a third times two by five plus four by nine plus two by nine which is a third of forty eight by forty five equals sixteen by forty five
total probability of red is sixteen by forty five
add the three routes with the common denominator forty five, the bracket is 48 by 45
P of red ante one by three into bracket, bracket 48 by 45, answer 16 by 45
the denominator of bayes is 16 by 45

steps.why: Red can come from any of three disjoint routes, so their probabilities add. The common factor 1/3 can be taken out first, which keeps the arithmetic to one fraction sum.

steps.label: Bayes' theorem

accept: P of B two given R is a third times four by nine over sixteen by forty five which is five by twelve
by bayes theorem the answer is five by twelve
the B two route four by twenty seven divided by the total sixteen by forty five gives five twelfths
bayes prakaram 4 by 27 ni 16 by 45 tho divide cheste 5 by 12
the probability it came from B two is five by twelve

steps.why: The B₂ route is the largest of the three (4/9 red), so its share of P(R) is the largest, and 5/12 is more than 1/3 — a quick check that the answer is in the right direction.
common_mistakes: Cancelling 4/27 · 45/16 wrongly — the answer is 180/432 = 5/12, not 5/4.
